topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Area and the distributive property
topic.description: Use tiling to demonstrate the distributive property: the area of a rectangle with sides a and (b+c) equals a×b + a×c; use area models to represent the distributive property
evidence: Tile a 3×(4+2) rectangle and show it decomposes into 3×4 and 3×2
Use an area model to compute 6×13 as 6×10 + 6×3
Draw an area model showing 5×(7+3) = 5×7 + 5×3
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to work out 6 × 13 by splitting it into 6 × 10 and 6 × 3, can they draw a rectangle divided into two parts to show why that method works?

pedagogy.summary: The area model makes the distributive property visible: a rectangle a×(b+c) split by a single line becomes two sub-rectangles a×b and a×c whose areas SUM to the whole. It is a representational bridge from area to symbolic multiplication — the same picture that shows 6×13 = 6×10 + 6×3 later underwrites partial products and long multiplication. It rests on spatial structuring (seeing the region as rows and columns) and on area being additive, both established earlier.
bestPractices: Start concrete: tile a rectangle, then physically cut it into two sub-rectangles and match each piece to a product and the whole to a×(b+c)
Always translate BOTH ways — read a given model into an equation, AND draw a model for a given equation — since the topic is representational fluency, not just computing
Split at a friendly number (the ten): 6×13 → 6×10 + 6×3, so the model becomes a calculation strategy
Keep the repeated factor visible on BOTH sub-rectangles (both parts are still 'a' units tall) to pre-empt the drop-the-factor error
Show that different splits of the same rectangle all recompose to the same total (additivity)
keyRepresentations: A partitioned rectangle / area model split into two labelled regions
The open array (regions labelled by dimensions, tiles not all drawn)
The aligned equation a×(b+c) = a×b + a×c written beside the picture
Row-strip cutouts for children still building the row/column structure
commonMisconceptions: Distributes to only one addend: 6×(10+3) = 6×10 + 3 (drops the ×6 on the second part)
Adds the side lengths instead of the region areas (6 + 13, or 10 + 3)
Cannot place the split so the two parts recompose to the whole — a spatial-structuring difficulty
Computes the two sub-areas but forgets to add them into the whole

learn.summary: Builds representational fluency between a partitioned rectangle (area model) and the distributive equation a×(b+c) = a×b + a×c. The same picture that shows 6×13 = 6×10 + 6×3 later underwrites partial products and long multiplication. Rests on spatial structuring (seeing a region as rows and columns) and on area being additive, both built earlier. Learners should translate BOTH ways — read a model into an equation and draw a model for an equation — and keep the repeated factor visible on both sub-rectangles.

activities.title: Cut the rectangle, keep the factor
feedback: If a piece is labelled just '3' instead of '3×4', point to its height: it is still 3 rows tall, so its area is 3×4, not 3.
If side numbers are added (e.g. 4+2) instead of areas, tile one sub-rectangle and count the squares inside to contrast a length (edge) with a region (area).
If the two sub-areas are found but not added, ask: 'You found the two parts — now what is the WHOLE rectangle worth?'
activities.rationale: Starting concrete with tiling and physical cutting grounds the additive, decomposition structure of area before symbols; keeping the height visible on both pieces pre-empts the drop-the-factor error.
sourceClaims: Students learn that the area of a 12-by-5 rectangle can be found either by 12×5 or by adding two products, e.g. 10×5 and 2×5, illustrating the distributive property; they use composition/decomposition, spatial structuring and addition of area measurements to investigate arithmetic properties with area models.

Area work rests on spatial structuring — seeing a region as rows and columns of squares; this is the key hurdle, needs many array activities, and incomplete arrays are where children struggle; row-strip cutouts and drawing/joining unit marks scaffold it.
learnerActions: Tile a 3×(4+2) rectangle (3 rows of 6 tiles), then physically cut it along the grid line between the first 4 columns and the last 2 columns, making two sub-rectangles.
Match each piece to its product (3×4 and 3×2) and match the whole uncut rectangle to 3×(4+2).
Say out loud how tall BOTH pieces are (still 3 rows), confirming the repeated factor appears on each part.
Recompose the pieces and check the two areas sum to the whole.
activities.intendedInsight: A rectangle a×(b+c) split by one line across its (b+c) side, at the point between b and c, becomes two sub-rectangles a×b and a×c whose areas SUM to the whole; the repeated factor 'a' stays on both parts.

activities.title: Split at the ten to make a hard fact easy
feedback: If the learner writes 6×13 = 6×10 + 3, point out the second region is still 6 rows tall, so it is 6×3 = 18, not 3.
If an awkward split appears to give a different total, re-tile or re-count: a correct split always recomposes to the same whole.
Prompt flexibility: 'Is one split easier to compute? Does choosing it change the answer?'
activities.rationale: Making the split a visible choice shows the model is a calculation strategy, not a trick, and demonstrating that different splits recompose to the same total reinforces area additivity. Moving from fully tiled to an open array previews partial products. A draggable split line that relabels regions and assembles the equation live is one optional way to make the choice and recomposition vivid.
sourceClaims: Students learn that the area of a 12-by-5 rectangle can be found either by 12×5 or by adding two products, e.g. 10×5 and 2×5, illustrating the distributive property; they use composition/decomposition, spatial structuring and addition of area measurements to investigate arithmetic properties with area models.
learnerActions: On a 6-by-13 rectangle on a grid, place one vertical split line under the '10'.
Label the two regions with their products (6×10 = 60 and 6×3 = 18) and write the matching equation 6×13 = 6×10 + 6×3 = 78 beside the picture.
Once comfortable, re-label the same partition as an open array — mark each region by its dimensions (6×10 and 6×3) without drawing every tile — as a step toward purely symbolic partial products.
Try a different split of the same rectangle (e.g. 6×7 and 6×6) and check the total is still 78.
Explain why splitting at the ten makes the calculation easier even though any valid split gives the same total.
activities.intendedInsight: Splitting at a friendly number (the ten) turns a hard product into two known facts; the split is a strategy the learner chooses, and different valid splits all recompose to the same total (additivity).

activities.title: Read it and draw it both ways
feedback: If the produced model shows 5×12 = 5×10 + 2, the second region is 5 rows tall → 5×2, not 2; the factor 5 belongs on both parts.
If the regions are read as loose squares or edge numbers, return to tiling one region and counting its area.

If the drawn regions overlap, leave gaps, or have widths that don't add to 12, offer row-strip cutouts or a pre-drawn grid and let the learner find where 12 = 10 + 2 falls before adding the equation on top. If the learner cuts across the 5 instead (e.g. 2×12 + 3×12), accept it as a valid split that still totals 60, then ask them to also try splitting the 12 so both pieces keep the factor 5.
activities.rationale: The topic is representational fluency, not just computing, so both the reading direction and the independent constructing direction are needed; a learner who draws 5×12 = 5×10 + 2 exposes the distributive misconception in their own diagram. A matching / fill-the-blank / find-the-error / draw-the-split response format can be used during teaching as well as for checking.
sourceClaims: Students learn that the area of a 12-by-5 rectangle can be found either by 12×5 or by adding two products, e.g. 10×5 and 2×5, illustrating the distributive property; they use composition/decomposition, spatial structuring and addition of area measurements to investigate arithmetic properties with area models.
Discussions must clearly distinguish the attribute of area from other attributes, notably length — grounding the error of adding side lengths instead of region areas.
learnerActions: Given a rectangle split into a shaded 6×10 region and a 6×3 region, state the multiplication each shaded part stands for and what they make together.
Given 5×12, draw your own area model, choose where to split it, and write the matching equation (e.g. splitting at the ten: 5×12 = 5×10 + 5×2 = 50 + 10 = 60).
Keep the factor 5 on BOTH sub-rectangles and recompose to the whole.
Examine a worked example such as '6×13 = 6×10 + 3', find the error, and say what was forgotten.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency means moving in both directions: reading a given model into an equation AND constructing a model for a given equation, keeping the common factor and recomposing to the whole.

activities.title: Reveal the parts, then the whole
feedback: If the learner stops after naming the two parts, ask what the whole rectangle is worth so they complete the recomposition.
If the whole is given as one region's value (e.g. 60, the 6×10 region, offered as the answer to 6×13), point to the second shaded region (6×3 = 18) that has not yet been added in.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal static model supports reading each region as a product and makes the 'remember to add the parts' step explicit; its limit is that pre-baked content cannot let the learner choose and draw their own split, so it is a scaffold toward independent production. Lift-the-flap / tap-to-reveal on each region is one optional way to stage the reveal.
learnerActions: On a static split area model of 6×13, reveal the left region's product (6×10 = 60), then the right region's (6×3 = 18).
Reveal the whole rectangle's value (6×13 = 78) and state in words that it is the two parts added.
Re-tell the chain: two parts → added → whole.
activities.intendedInsight: The whole area equals the sum of the two sub-areas; revealing them in sequence makes the 'add the parts' step explicit.

constraints: Translate in BOTH directions: reading a model into an equation alone is not sufficient; learners must also construct a model for a given equation.
Keep the repeated factor on BOTH sub-rectangles to pre-empt the drop-the-factor error (6×13 = 6×10 + 3).
Distinguish the attribute of area (region/tiles inside) from length (edges) to prevent adding side lengths instead of region areas.
A static tap-to-reveal model is a scaffold: it supports reading regions as products but does not by itself elicit the learner's own choice of split or independent drawing.

Do not impose the equation on a partition the learner cannot yet see: if they cannot place a split that recomposes to the whole, give row-strip cutouts or a pre-drawn grid and coordinate with array practice first.
Interactive examples (a draggable split line, live relabelling, running products, lift-the-flap) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory mechanisms.
Recognition/reveal-only responses do not by themselves elicit independent construction of a model; include at least one task where the learner draws and writes their own split.
The area model is planar for this objective; this does not establish that other media cannot teach it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Confirmed the incomplete-recomposition feedback in the reveal activity is consistent with its 6×13 setup: 60 is the 6×10 region offered as the whole, not a wrong claim about 5×12.
Restored the open array as an optional intermediate representation in the split-at-the-ten activity, since it was a named representation in the original research.

The original marked 3D and conversation media as 'poor'; those catalog comparisons are softened to the objective point that the area model is planar for this objective, without universal-necessity or medium-superiority claims.
The Year 4 National Curriculum age-placement claim is flagged verified:false in the row; treated as unverified and not used as a sourceClaim.

probeDeeper: 'Why did you split the 12 into 10 and 2, and not into 6 and 6? Is one easier — and does it change the answer?'
'Here's a model split into 6×10 and 6×3, but someone wrote 6×13 = 6×10 + 3. What did they forget?' (surfaces the drop-the-factor error on a fresh case)
'Show me on the picture where the ×6 is hiding in BOTH parts.'
'Could you split 5×12 a different way and still get 60? Show me.' (tests flexibility and additivity)

errorPatterns.pattern: Distributes to only one addend — reads or writes 6×13 = 6×10 + 3, labelling the second region just '3' instead of '6×3' (drops the repeated factor)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to tiles: show the second sub-rectangle is still 6 (or 5) rows tall, so its area is 6×3 not 3; label the repeated side on BOTH regions.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In the produce tier writes 5×12 = 5×10 + 2, or in the interpret tier names the second part '3' rather than '6×3'

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds the side lengths instead of the region areas — reads the whole as 6 + 13, or the parts as 10 + 3
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast a length (an edge) with a region (the tiles inside); tile one sub-rectangle so the child counts area, not edges.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sums edge numbers rather than the shaded areas; answer looks like a perimeter or a length total

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot place a split that recomposes to the whole — the drawn split line doesn't correspond to 10+2, fragments the repeated factor, or they can't partition at all
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT impose the equation on top of a partition they can't yet see; give row-strip cutouts or a pre-drawn grid and let them find where 12 = 10 + 2 falls — this coordinates with array practice and self-corrects.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In the produce tier draws overlapping/unequal regions, a split that doesn't total 12, or a horizontal cut that breaks the ×5

errorPatterns.pattern: Splits correctly but forgets to recompose — computes the two sub-products and stops, offering one region as 'the answer'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold: 'You found the two parts — now what is the WHOLE rectangle worth?' — a prompt to complete, not a reteach.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Finds 5×10 = 50 and 5×2 = 10 but doesn't add them, or gives 50 as the answer to 5×12

responseLevels.gap: Reads the regions only as loose squares or as edge numbers; when asked to produce a model, cannot partition or drops the common factor (writes 5×10 + 2).
responseLevels.full: Interprets each region as a product AND independently chooses a friendly split, keeps the repeated factor across both regions, and recomposes to the whole (5×12 = 5×10 + 5×2 = 60), transferring the move to a new product.
responseLevels.partial: Reads both regions as products and can draw a split, but treats the two facts as separate — lists 5×10 and 5×2 without joining them into 5×12, or can only work from a split that is handed to them.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show an area model of 6 × 13: a rectangle split by one line into a shaded 6×10 region and a differently-shaded 6×3 region. FIRST (interpret): 'This picture shows 6 × 13. Point to the two parts — what multiplication does each shaded part stand for, and what happens when you put them together?' THEN (translate/produce): 'Now here is 5 × 12. Draw an area model that splits it to make it easier to work out, and write the matching equation.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The interpret tier catches whether the child sees each region as a PRODUCT (not just loose squares or edge numbers); the produce tier catches whether they can choose a useful split AND keep the common factor across both parts. A child who draws 5×12 = 5×10 + 2 exposes the distributive misconception in their own diagram — a translation task makes the error visible without having to ask about it.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Understanding Area
topic.description: Understand that a unit square has one square unit of area and that the area of a plane figure is the number of unit squares that cover it without gaps or overlaps
evidence: Identify a unit square and state its area is 1 square unit
Explain why a figure covered by 12 unit squares has area 12 square units
Distinguish between area and perimeter as different measurements
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} counts the small squares inside a rectangle drawn on squared paper, can they tell you the area — and explain what "one square unit" means?

pedagogy.summary: Area is the amount of two-dimensional surface inside a bounded region, measured by choosing a unit of area — usually a square — and finding how many unit squares cover the figure with no gaps or overlaps. A unit square has an area of 1 square unit; a figure covered by 12 unit squares has area 12 square units. The concept must be held distinct from perimeter (the distance around) and understood as unchanged when the same squares are rearranged.
bestPractices: Start from covering: which of several shapes covers the most surface, first by cutting/re-composing, then by covering with unit squares.
Name the unit square as '1 square unit' and area as the count of such squares that cover the region without gaps or overlaps.

Deliberately separate area from perimeter — on congruent rectangles, label the unit lengths around the edge of one and draw the square units inside the other, so the two measures are visibly different.
Establish that area is additive and unchanged under rearrangement: the same tiles cover the same area however you move them.
Use square-unit language in every answer ('12 square centimetres', not '12').
keyRepresentations: A single unit square labelled '1 square unit'
A figure on squared paper filled with unit squares, counted
Congruent rectangles: one with unit lengths marked round the perimeter, one with the interior square units drawn
The same set of tiles rearranged into different shapes (area conserved, perimeter changes)
commonMisconceptions: Confuses area with perimeter / length — judges the 'bigger' shape by how far it stretches or the distance around, not the surface covered.
Undifferentiated 'bigger' — calls a longer or taller shape bigger by one dimension without coordinating the 2D covering.
Thinks rearranging the same squares into a new shape changes the amount of area.
Gives area as a bare number without square units, or counts squares with gaps/overlaps.

learn.summary: Area is the amount of two-dimensional surface inside a bounded region, measured by counting how many unit squares (the usual chosen unit of area) cover the figure with no gaps or overlaps. A unit square has area 1 square unit; a figure covered by 12 unit squares has area 12 square units. The concept must be held distinct from perimeter (the distance around) and understood as unchanged when the same squares are rearranged (area is additive and conserved under recomposition). Answers should always carry square-unit language.

activities.title: Cover, count, and separate area from perimeter
feedback: If the squares leave gaps or overlap, say: area is only valid when the squares tile the region with no gaps and no overlaps — line them up edge-to-edge and count again.
If a child gives area as a bare number, prompt: 12 what? Area is counted in square units — say '12 square units' (or '12 square centimetres').

After rearranging, if a child expects the area to change, re-count the tiles together: the same 12 squares still cover 12 square units. Only the shape's outline changed, and the perimeter may or may not have changed, so count it to check.

When area and perimeter are confused, point to the filled interior (area, in square units) versus the traced edge (perimeter, in unit lengths) on the same shape so the two measures are visibly different.
activities.rationale: Building area from physically covering a region with unit squares, then separately tracing the edge, makes 'surface covered' versus 'distance around' concrete, and recomposing the same tiles exhibits conservation of area. An optional live square-unit counter and an AREA/PERIMETER toggle (interior fill vs edge trace) and a rearrange mode can make the distinction and the conservation vivid, but the same learning works with squared paper and physical square tiles.
sourceClaims: Area is the amount of two-dimensional space in a bounded region, measured by choosing a unit of area (often a square); a figure covered by a certain number of squares without gaps or overlaps has an area of that number of square units (3.MD.5, 3.MD.6). Area measurement assumes congruent figures enclose equal areas and that area is additive.
learnerActions: Fill a figure drawn on squared paper with unit squares, snapping them edge-to-edge with no gaps or overlaps, and count them to state the area, e.g. 'area = 12 square units'.

Trace the boundary of the SAME shape separately, stepping round the edge and counting the unit lengths, and record the perimeter in unit lengths. This is a different kind of measure from the area. For a 12-square figure the perimeter number is also different (at least 14), but for some shapes the two numbers can match: a 4-by-4 square has area 16 square units and perimeter 16 units. Even then they measure different things.
Say aloud that the squares INSIDE measure area while the steps AROUND measure perimeter — two different measures of the same shape.

Rearrange the same set of (e.g. 12) tiles, joined edge-to-edge, into a long strip. Re-count the covering squares (still 12), then re-count the perimeter and compare. For example, a 3-by-4 rectangle has perimeter 14 units, but a 1-by-12 strip has perimeter 26 units. The area count stays the same whether or not the perimeter changes.
activities.intendedInsight: Area is the count of unit squares covering a region; it is distinct from perimeter and is unchanged when the same squares are rearranged.

activities.title: Label area on one rectangle, perimeter on its congruent twin
feedback: If a child treats the edge count and the interior count as the same kind of number, highlight the units: one is in square units, the other in unit lengths.
If a child insists a shape with a longer edge must have more area, set up a long-thin shape and a compact shape and count the covering squares to settle it directly.
activities.rationale: Deliberately pairing a perimeter-labelled rectangle with an identical area-filled rectangle addresses the common area/perimeter confusion by making each measure visible on congruent figures.
sourceClaims: Students initially hold undifferentiated views of measurable attributes, calling one object 'bigger' whether it is longer, greater in area, or greater in volume; discussions must clearly distinguish area from length. With strong, distinct concepts of area and perimeter, students differentiate them by drawing rectangles with the same perimeter but different areas (or vice versa) and by labelling unit lengths around the perimeter of one congruent rectangle while drawing the square units inside another.
learnerActions: Take two congruent rectangles.
On the first, mark the unit lengths all the way around the perimeter and total them.
On the second, draw the interior square units and count them for the area.
State in words how the two measurements differ, using square units for area and unit lengths for perimeter.
activities.intendedInsight: Area (surface covered, in square units) and perimeter (distance around, in unit lengths) are distinct attributes even of the very same rectangle.

activities.title: Predict then count: does longer mean bigger area?
feedback: If a child picks the long strip because 'it stretches further', count the squares in both: here the compact Shape A has 12 squares and the strip Shape B has 10, so A has the bigger area despite stretching less (and B even has the longer perimeter).
If a child gets the right answer but justifies it with 'it looks chunkier', push them to count the covering squares so the reason rests on the unit-square count.
For a rearrangement claim that area changed, recompose the identical tiles and re-count — the number of covering squares is unchanged.
activities.rationale: A predict-then-count comparison surfaces and confronts the 'longer/more spread-out is bigger' misconception, and the reasoning prompts distinguish genuine understanding from a lucky choice. Note that in the compact-12 vs strip-10 case the compact shape also has the larger area, so 'bigger area' coincides with 'more compact'; the reasoning tier plus the same-tiles rearrangement probe (same squares, area unchanged) is what truly discriminates. The chosen case does make the shape with the longer perimeter (the strip) the one with the smaller area, so area/perimeter confusion leads to the wrong pick.
sourceClaims: Students initially hold undifferentiated views of measurable attributes, calling one object 'bigger' whether it is longer, greater in area, or greater in volume; discussions must clearly distinguish area from length. With strong, distinct concepts of area and perimeter, students differentiate them by drawing rectangles with the same perimeter but different areas (or vice versa) and by labelling unit lengths around the perimeter of one congruent rectangle while drawing the square units inside another.
learnerActions: Before counting, look at two shapes — a compact block and a long spread-out strip — and predict which has the bigger area and why.
Count the covering unit squares in each shape.
Compare your prediction with the counts and explain any difference.

Answer the follow-ups: What does the area of a shape actually tell you? If you cut a shape apart and rearrange its squares into a long line, does the area change? Why? Shape B is longer than Shape A — so why doesn't 'longer' mean 'bigger area'? How is area different from the distance all the way around the edge?
activities.intendedInsight: 'Bigger area' is decided by counting covering squares, not by how far a shape stretches or how long its edge is; and area is preserved when the same squares are rearranged.

activities.title: Sort statements: about area or about perimeter?
feedback: If a shape with a bigger perimeter is assumed to have a bigger area, revisit the long-thin-vs-compact pair where the bigger-perimeter shape has the smaller area.
Reinforce square-unit language for every area answer.
activities.rationale: Classification and comparison items are discriminating checks of the concept and its distinction from perimeter; they work as a consolidation check after hands-on covering. As a recognition-style check a sort can assess and reinforce the area/perimeter distinction, but it does not by itself require the learner to construct and conserve area, so pair it with the covering and rearranging work.
learnerActions: Read statements and shape comparisons and sort each into 'about area' or 'about perimeter'.
For a long-thin shape and a compact shape, decide which has the bigger area and which has the bigger perimeter, and justify each by counting.
Choose, with reasons, which of several shapes has the bigger area.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can tell which questions concern surface covered (area) versus distance around (perimeter) and justify comparisons by counting.

constraints: Area answers must always be stated in square units (e.g. '12 square centimetres'), not as a bare number.
Unit squares must tile the region with no gaps and no overlaps for the count to be a valid area.

Static reference images (a labelled '1 square unit' and a 12-square figure marked 'area = 12 square units') are useful consolidation but do not let a learner rearrange tiles to experience conservation; pair them with hands-on covering and recomposition.

A sort/multiple-choice check can assess and reinforce the area/perimeter distinction but is a recognition task; it does not by itself require independent construction or demonstrate conservation of area, so use it alongside covering and rearranging activities.
Keep the focus on 2D surface. A 3D setting risks conflating area with volume; if 3D is used, keep the measured attribute explicitly the flat surface.
The optional live counter, AREA/PERIMETER toggle, and rearrange mode are helpful illustrations of the mechanism, not required mechanisms; squared paper and physical tiles achieve the same objective.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Original internal tension: the POE task specifies two shapes with the SAME number of unit squares (to confront conservation), while the diagnostic uses Shape A = 3×4 = 12 squares vs Shape B = 1×10 = 10 squares. The learner activity uses the diagnostic counts (where the strip also has the longer perimeter and smaller area); the reasoning tier and the same-tiles rearrangement probe (area stays 12, perimeter changes) are the stronger discriminators. Both the comparison and the conservation probe are retained.

Categorical catalog judgements that static content, dialogue, or 3D 'cannot' teach the concept are retained only as scoped limits (static images do not support rearrangement; a 3D setting risks volume confusion), not as universal claims about what a medium can teach.
Whether rearranging the 12 tiles changes the perimeter depends on the outline; it is asserted only for the specific 3×4→1×12 strip example used.
Source 'verified:true' flags and 'high' confidence are legacy metadata not re-checked in this rewrite.

assess.poeTask: Before any counting, show two shapes made from the SAME number of unit squares — one a compact block, one a long spread-out strip — and ask the child to predict which has the bigger area and WHY. Then have them count the squares in each. The equal counts confront a 'the longer/more spread-out one is bigger' prediction; the target explanation, given after counting, is that the same squares cover the same amount of surface however they are arranged.
probeDeeper: What does the area of a shape actually tell you?
If I cut Shape A apart and rearrange its 12 squares into a long line, does it still have the same area? Why?
Shape B is longer than Shape A — so why doesn't 'longer' mean 'bigger area' here?
How is the area of a shape different from the distance all the way around its edge?
assess.correctAnswer: Shape A. Area is the number of unit squares that cover a shape with no gaps or overlaps, and A is covered by 12 squares while B is covered by 10 — so A has the bigger area, 12 square units, even though B stretches further.

errorPatterns.pattern: Area/perimeter confusion: judges 'bigger' by how far the shape stretches or the distance around its edge, so chooses the long strip.
errorPatterns.nextMove: On congruent rectangles, mark the unit lengths around the perimeter of one and draw the square units inside the other, so the child sees area (surface covered) and perimeter (distance around) are different measures; then count squares to compare.
errorPatterns.distractor: Shape B, the long strip — it stretches much further, so it covers more.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks Shape B and justifies with 'it stretches further' or 'it has a longer edge/goes further round'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Undifferentiated 'bigger' by one dimension: calls the longer shape bigger from a single dimension without coordinating the two-dimensional covering.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare a single object's several attributes (how long? how much surface?) to distinguish them; count the covering squares to decide area.
errorPatterns.distractor: Shape B, because it is longer than Shape A.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses Shape B 'because it is longer than A', attending only to length.

errorPatterns.pattern: Non-conservation of area: believes rearranging the same squares into a different shape changes the amount of area.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Recompose the identical tiles and re-count — the number of covering squares is unchanged; area is preserved under rearrangement (area is additive).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: In the rearrangement probe, says the spread-out shape has more (or less) area than the compact one made from the same squares.

responseLevels.gap: Judges 'bigger' by length, perimeter or how far the shape stretches, choosing the long strip.
responseLevels.full: Defines area as the number of unit squares covering the figure with no gaps or overlaps, compares by counting, holds it distinct from perimeter/length, and knows the area is unchanged when the same squares are rearranged.
responseLevels.partial: Counts unit squares to compare and gets the right answer, but the area/perimeter distinction is shaky — also thinks a longer edge means more area, or is unsure the area stays the same when the squares are rearranged.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show two shapes on squared paper: Shape A is a solid 3-by-4 block (12 squares) and Shape B is a long 1-by-10 strip (10 squares). Ask: 'Which shape has the bigger AREA — and how do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The answer alone can be guessed, so the reason tier carries it: a child who understands area counts the covering squares and picks A; a child who confuses area with length or perimeter picks the long strip B because it 'goes further'. pedagogy.summary: Perimeter is the total distance around the boundary of a 2-D shape, found by measuring every side and adding the lengths (or, for a regular shape, multiplying one side by the number of sides). The concept to secure is that perimeter is a length — the once-around distance — and is distinct from area (the surface covered inside).
bestPractices: Define perimeter physically as walking all the way around the edge and back to the start.
Measure and label every side, then add — for a rectangle, remind pupils the two unmarked sides equal their opposites.
For regular shapes, connect equal sides to multiplication (side length × number of sides).
Deliberately contrast perimeter (distance around) with area (surface covered) on the same shape so the two are not confused.
Keep the length unit in the answer (cm, m).
keyRepresentations: A shape with each side measured and labelled, summed around the boundary
A finger/marker tracing the whole boundary back to the start
A regular polygon: one side labelled, perimeter = side × number of sides
A rectangle with only two adjacent sides given, the opposite two to be filled in
commonMisconceptions: Adds only the two given sides of a rectangle, forgetting the opposite two.
Confuses perimeter with area — counts the squares inside instead of the distance around.
For a regular shape, measures one side but doesn't account for all the equal sides.
Gives the perimeter as a bare number without a length unit.

learn.summary: Perimeter is the total distance once around the boundary of a 2-D shape — found by measuring every side and adding the lengths, or for a regular shape multiplying one side by the number of sides. The core idea to secure is that perimeter is a length (the once-around distance) and is distinct from area (the surface covered inside). Target age 7–8.

activities.title: Walk the boundary and build the total
feedback: If a child adds only the two given sides of a rectangle, have them first label the two opposite sides (which equal their partners), then add all four; trace the full boundary to check nothing is missed.

If a child reports the number of squares inside or an area figure, contrast the two measures on the same shape — trace the boundary for perimeter, shade the interior for area — and name which the question asks for.
If a child gives only one side of a regular polygon, establish that it has n equal sides so perimeter = side × n, and check the number of sides.
If the total is correct but the unit is missing, treat the answer as incomplete and build the habit of writing cm/m; the adding itself is sound.
activities.rationale: Tracing the boundary makes 'distance around' concrete; hiding two rectangle sides forces the learner to supply the equal opposite sides, directly targeting the most common error; a regular-shape step links equal sides to multiplication. An optional interactive version — dragging a marker so each side lights and its length clicks into a running total that will not advance past a hidden side until the opposite side is supplied, plus an area/perimeter shading toggle and a regular-polygon side×n mode — makes the once-around mechanism visible, but the same learning works with paper shapes, a ruler and labelled drawings.
sourceClaims: The perimeter of a polygon is the sum of the lengths of its sides. For rectangles and parallelograms often only two adjacent side lengths are given, and the common error is to add just those two numbers; having students first label the lengths of the other two sides is a helpful reminder. For regular polygons the perimeter is the product of one side length and the number of sides.
learnerActions: Trace a finger or marker all the way around the edge of a shape, starting and finishing at the same corner, so 'perimeter' is felt as walking once around and back to the start.
On a rectangle that shows only two adjacent side lengths, work out the two hidden opposite sides (opposite sides are equal), label them, then add all four sides.
Keep a running total as you cover each side, and only count the perimeter as complete when the whole boundary has been traced back to the start.
On a regular pentagon with one side labelled, find the perimeter as side length × 5 (or by adding five equal sides) and explain why the shortcut works.
Measure every side of a small irregular shape with a ruler and add the lengths.
Write each answer with its length unit (cm or m).
activities.intendedInsight: Perimeter is the complete once-around distance: you must account for every side (including hidden equal ones), it is a length with a unit, and for a regular shape equal sides let you multiply instead of adding one by one.

activities.title: Perimeter is not area
feedback: If the learner counts interior squares when asked for perimeter, point back to the boundary trace: perimeter follows only the edge.
If they are unsure which is asked, have them underline the word 'around' or 'covered/inside' in the question and match it to the correct action.
activities.rationale: Distinguishing area from perimeter is a distinction that must be maintained; deliberately performing both on the same shape makes the contrast explicit and discriminating.
sourceClaims: With strong, distinct concepts of perimeter and area, students differentiate the two measures; abstraction underscores the importance of distinguishing area from perimeter, a distinction that must be maintained across grades.
learnerActions: On one straight-sided shape drawn along the lines of a square grid, first trace the boundary and add the side lengths to find the perimeter, then shade the interior and count the unit squares to find the area (in square units).
State in your own words which measure is a distance around the edge and which is the surface covered inside.
Given a question, decide whether it is asking for perimeter or area before you start, and say how you know.
activities.intendedInsight: Perimeter (distance around the edge, a length) and area (surface covered inside) are different measures on the very same shape and must not be swapped.

activities.title: Spot-the-error and mixed practice
feedback: For the spot-the-error item, confirm the fix is to add all four sides after supplying the equal opposite pair.
For the area distractor, confirm the learner traced the boundary rather than counting interior squares.
Flag any missing unit as an incomplete answer.
activities.rationale: Discriminating items — a two-sides-given rectangle, a side×n regular polygon, a spot-the-error on adding only two sides, and a perimeter-vs-area distractor — target the documented errors. These check and reinforce the procedure; use them alongside, not instead of, hands-on measuring and summing.
sourceClaims: The perimeter of a polygon is the sum of the lengths of its sides. For rectangles and parallelograms often only two adjacent side lengths are given, and the common error is to add just those two numbers; having students first label the lengths of the other two sides is a helpful reminder. For regular polygons the perimeter is the product of one side length and the number of sides.
learnerActions: Solve fill-the-blank items: a rectangle with only two adjacent sides given (supply the opposite two, then total), and a regular polygon with one side labelled (use side × number of sides).
Judge a worked example where another child added only the two given rectangle sides — say what went wrong and give the correct perimeter.
Answer a mixed item where one option is the area of the shape, choosing and justifying the correct perimeter.
Check every answer carries its length unit.
activities.intendedInsight: Applying perimeter across rectangle (hidden sides), regular-polygon (side×n), and perimeter-vs-area cases, and critiquing a wrong method, consolidates accurate, unit-bearing reasoning.

constraints: Keep the length unit (cm, m) in every perimeter answer; a bare number is incomplete. Area answers use square units (e.g. square centimetres or 'squares'), not length units.

A static labelled shape with the boundary highlighted can illustrate 'distance around', but it does not let the learner rehearse measuring and summing all sides — use it as a reference, not as the main practice.
Recognition-only or multiple-choice items check and reinforce the procedure but do not by themselves elicit independent measuring and summing; pair them with hands-on construction.
When using a regular-shape shortcut, first establish how many equal sides the shape has, so side × n is justified rather than guessed.
For a rectangle with only two adjacent sides given, require the learner to supply the opposite two sides before totalling; do not let them stop at the two given numbers.

assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands perimeter accounts for every side and gives a once-around length; a child who does not adds only the two given rectangle sides, counts the squares inside (area), or uses just one side of the regular shape — each visible in the working.

pedagogy.summary: Perimeter problem-solving extends 'perimeter = sum of all sides' in two directions: working backwards to find an unknown side (total minus the known sides), and dissociating perimeter from area (rectangles with the same perimeter can have very different areas). It rests on securely measuring perimeter and on labelling every side before adding.
bestPractices: Insist on labelling ALL sides before adding — the documented remedy for the 'add just the two given sides' error
For an unknown side, reason 'perimeter total − sum of known sides = missing side' (a total-minus-parts / bar-model move)

Explore same-perimeter-different-area on grid paper (e.g. the 'robot on grid paper' activity): sketch several rectangles of fixed perimeter and tabulate their areas so the two attributes visibly come apart

learn.summary: Perimeter problem-solving for ages 8–9 extends 'perimeter = sum of all sides' in two directions: working backwards to find an unknown side (total minus the known sides), and separating perimeter from area (rectangles with the same perimeter can have very different areas). It rests on labelling every side before adding and keeping units explicit (cm for perimeter, cm² for area).

activities.title: Watch the area change while the perimeter stays the same
feedback: If the learner claims rectangles of equal perimeter 'must' have the same area, have them actually count the interior squares of two of their tabulated shapes — the counts differ, showing area varies while perimeter stays put.
If two of the tabulated shapes come out the same (congruent), prompt: 'Make one much longer and thinner but keep the every-side total at 24 cm,' then re-tabulate the area.
Reinforce keeping cm with perimeter and cm² with area so the two attributes stay distinct.
activities.rationale: The CCSS progression has students find and sketch rectangles with the same perimeter and different areas and justify their claims, making the length/area distinction explicit. A live grid where a dragged corner updates a perimeter/area table side by side (an OPTIONAL interaction example, not required) can make this variation visible, but tabulating several rectangles on grid paper achieves the same comparison.
sourceClaims: With distinct concepts of perimeter and area established, students find and sketch rectangles with the same perimeter and different areas (and vice versa) and justify their claims (e.g. the 'robot on grid paper' activity); the length/area distinction must be made explicit.
learnerActions: On a 1 cm square grid, draw or take a rectangle (e.g. one with perimeter 24 cm, starting as 5 cm × 7 cm) and record its perimeter and its area in a table with columns for length, width, perimeter and area.
Reshape it to become long and thin while keeping the same perimeter of 24 cm — e.g. go from 5×7 to 1×11 — and record the new area in a fresh row each time.
Compare the rows: notice the perimeter stays at 24 cm while the area changes (e.g. from 35 cm² down to 11 cm²).
Answer: if I only tell you a rectangle's perimeter is 24 cm, can you tell me its area for certain? Explain why not.
activities.intendedInsight: A fixed perimeter does not fix the area: rectangles with the same perimeter can have very different areas (although the perimeter still limits how big the area can get, e.g. no 24 cm rectangle has an area above 36 cm²).

activities.title: Label every side, then add
feedback: If the learner writes 8 + 5 = 13, point back to the unlabelled sides: 'You have not gone all the way around — what are the other two sides?' then re-add to 26 cm.

If the learner multiplies (8 × 5 = 40, which is the area, not the perimeter), distinguish the measures: on one copy of the rectangle count unit lengths all around the edge (perimeter); on an identical copy draw and count the squares inside (area) — they measure different things.
A static labelled polygon with a tap/lift-the-flap to reveal each side can drill the labelling habit; note it only rehearses that habit and does not show the perimeter/area variation.
activities.rationale: When a rectangle problem gives only two adjacent sides, the documented remedy is to have students first label the other two sides; the formula P = 2(l + w) is emphasised in later work precisely because it counters adding only one length and one width.
sourceClaims: When a rectangle problem gives only two adjacent side lengths, the common error is to add just those two numbers; having students first label the other two sides is the remedy. Students then find unknown side lengths in 'missing measurements' problems.

In Grade 4 the same error persists; the formula P = 2(l + w) is emphasised because it counters the usual error of adding only one length and one width, underscoring the Grade-3 importance of distinguishing area from perimeter.
learnerActions: Take a rectangle marked only 8 cm along the top and 5 cm down one side.
Before adding anything, label the two unmarked sides — each equals its opposite side (so 8 cm and 5 cm).
Add all four sides: 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 cm, and write the answer with its unit (cm).
Repeat for a polygon where only some sides are printed: fill in every side length you can determine, then add them all.
activities.intendedInsight: Perimeter is the sum of ALL sides; marking every side first prevents the common error of adding only the two given numbers.

activities.title: Find the missing side by reversing
feedback: If the learner adds the total into the sum (5 + 6 + 7 + 4 + 30), prompt: 'The 30 is the whole trip around — it is not one more side. What do the pieces have to add up to?'
If the learner freezes, scaffold with the bar: 'What must all the sides add to? How much do we already have? So the last piece is…' — this is a strategy prompt, not a reteach of perimeter.
Optionally confirm with a dynamic shape where one side is blank and a target perimeter is shown, dragging the edge until the shape closes (an OPTIONAL interaction example, not required).
activities.rationale: The progression has students find unknown side lengths in 'missing measurements' problems once perimeter is secure; a total-minus-parts move makes the reversal explicit as a strategy.
sourceClaims: When a rectangle problem gives only two adjacent side lengths, the common error is to add just those two numbers; having students first label the other two sides is the remedy. Students then find unknown side lengths in 'missing measurements' problems.
learnerActions: Take a shape with a known total perimeter but one side blank — e.g. a pentagon with perimeter 30 cm and four sides of 5 cm, 6 cm, 7 cm and 4 cm.
Add the known sides: 5 + 6 + 7 + 4 = 22 cm.
Subtract from the total to find the missing side: 30 − 22 = 8 cm.
Use a total-minus-parts bar or number line to narrate: 'All sides must total 30 cm; I already have 22 cm; so the last piece is 8 cm.'
Explain in your own words why you subtract rather than add here.
activities.intendedInsight: An unknown side is the perimeter total minus the sum of the known sides — a total-minus-parts (bar-model) reversal of finding the perimeter.

activities.title: Draw and justify same-perimeter, different-area pairs
feedback: If the learner draws two congruent rectangles or produces only one and claims any other 'must have the same area', run the grid-paper 'robot' activity: sketch several rectangles all of perimeter 24 cm and tabulate their areas so the area visibly changes while the perimeter stays fixed.
Ask for evidence of the perimeter claim: 'How do you know both are 24 cm?' — expect a count around each edge.
Praise correct unit use (cm vs cm²) as part of keeping the two attributes distinct.
activities.rationale: Constructing and justifying same-perimeter-different-area rectangles (and the reverse) is the explicit CCSS activity for making the length/area distinction robust; requiring the learner to draw and justify, not merely recognise, elicits independent construction. (Recognition/matching can expose the pattern but does not itself require construction.)
sourceClaims: With distinct concepts of perimeter and area established, students find and sketch rectangles with the same perimeter and different areas (and vice versa) and justify their claims (e.g. the 'robot on grid paper' activity); the length/area distinction must be made explicit.
learnerActions: On grid paper, draw TWO genuinely different rectangles that both have a perimeter of 24 cm (e.g. 1×11 and 5×7).
Work out the area of each (11 cm² and 35 cm²) and record perimeter in cm and area in cm².
Check your evidence: count the unit lengths around each rectangle to confirm both really measure 24 cm.
State in words: equal perimeter does not force equal area.
Extend (reverse case): try to find two rectangles with the same AREA but different perimeters, and show one pair.
activities.intendedInsight: A child who truly grasps the dissociation can construct two different rectangles of equal perimeter with unequal areas — and vice versa — and justify it, rather than just stating a rule.

constraints: Keep the unit with every number and answer: cm for perimeter, cm² for area, so the length/area distinction stays explicit.
Insist on labelling every side before adding — this is the documented remedy for the 'add only the two given sides' error.

A static labelled polygon with tap-to-reveal only rehearses the labelling habit; it cannot, on its own, run the same-perimeter-different-area comparison, which needs multiple rectangles drawn and compared (on grid paper or via a live model).

Recognition/matching tasks (e.g. matching rectangles to their perimeter/area pairs) can expose the dissociation but do not require the learner to construct rectangles; use construction tasks to elicit independent production.
The same-perimeter-different-area insight depends on actually comparing several shapes and their measures; do not reduce it to a stated rule.

Dynamic-model interaction examples (dragging a corner with a live perimeter/area table, blanking a side against a target) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory; grid paper and tables achieve the same learning.

Arithmetic re-checked in this independent pass: rectangle 8×5 perimeter = 8+5+8+5 = 26 cm; pentagon missing side = 30 − (5+6+7+4=22) = 8 cm; 1×11 has perimeter 24 cm and area 11 cm²; 5×7 has perimeter 24 cm and area 35 cm²; 8×5 = 40 cm² is the area, not the perimeter. The original '3D adds nothing' and 'an in-role dialogue partner cannot let the child measure/draw/reverse-solve' statements were catalog fit judgements, not established efficacy facts, and are not asserted as universal laws here. Perimeter of a plane polygon is two-dimensional, so a construct-and-compute approach on a flat grid is a natural fit, but this is a scoped observation, not a proof that other media cannot contribute.
The NC England (Year 4) claim is marked verified:false in the source; it is used only to confirm the age-appropriateness of finding an unknown side and should be treated as unconfirmed.

learn.summary: Year 5 pupils measure and calculate the perimeter of composite rectilinear shapes (straight sides, with every corner made by sides meeting at right angles — rectangles joined, e.g. an L-shape). The distinctive skill is DEDUCING unmarked side lengths from the labelled ones: in each direction, the side lengths on one side of the shape add up to the side lengths on the opposite side. In an L-shape this means the two shorter sides along one direction add up to the opposite longer side (so a missing length is found by adding the two shorter sides, or by subtracting a known shorter side from the longer one); other shapes, such as U- or T-shapes, may have more than two parts on one side. Pupils then total every boundary side exactly once. Chief hazards: adding only the given numbers (forgetting missing sides), working out a missing length wrongly, including internal split-lines, double-counting a side, and confusing perimeter (a length in cm or m) with area (cm2 or m2).

pedagogy.summary: Children come to see that area and perimeter are INDEPENDENT: two shapes can share an area yet have different perimeters, and share a perimeter yet have different areas. The work is systematic — fix one quantity (say area 24 cm²) and generate rectangles that differ in perimeter (a long thin 1×24 has a large perimeter; a squarer 4×6 a smaller one). The misconception to dislodge is the intuitive 'Same A – Same B' rule (same area must mean same perimeter, and vice versa). It is best taught by having children build many shapes with a fixed area or perimeter and tabulate the other, so the variation is SEEN, not asserted — and by probing reasoning, since a correct answer can still come from the faulty intuition.
bestPractices: Fix one quantity and vary the shape systematically (all rectangles of area 24; all shapes of perimeter 20), tabulating the other so children see it change.
Confront the 'Same A – Same B' intuition head-on with counterexamples (a 3×4 and a 2×6 rectangle both have area 12 but perimeters 14 and 16).
Use squared paper and tiles so children construct and count rather than rely on a remembered rule.
Probe reasoning beyond correct answers — a right answer can come from the intuitive rule, so always ask 'why' (Tsamir & Mandel).
Link to practical intuition: a long thin field and a square field can hold the same crop area but need very different lengths of fence.

learn.summary: Children learn that knowing one of area or perimeter does NOT determine the other: two shapes can share an area yet have different perimeters, and share a perimeter yet have different areas. The core work is systematic — fix one quantity (e.g. area 24 cm²) and generate shapes that differ in the other, tabulating so the variation is SEEN, not asserted. The target misconception is the intuitive 'Same A – Same B' rule (same area must mean same perimeter, and vice versa). topic.name: Area of compound shapes
topic.description: Recognise area as additive; find areas of rectilinear figures by decomposing into non-overlapping rectangles and summing their areas

pedagogy.summary: Because area is additive, a rectilinear figure (an L- or T-shape) can be cut into non-overlapping rectangles, each area found by multiplying, then summed. The two hard steps are partitioning cleanly (no gaps, no overlaps) and deriving a sub-rectangle's missing side from the outer measurements. It is a direct application of area-as-additive and of finding rectangle areas by multiplying.

learn.summary: Teaches children to find the area of compound rectilinear shapes (L- and T-shapes) by decomposing them into non-overlapping rectangles, finding each rectangle's area by multiplying, and summing. The two hard steps are partitioning cleanly (no gaps, no overlaps) and deriving a sub-rectangle's missing internal side from the given outer measurements. This rests on two prior ideas: area is additive, and rectangle area is found by multiplying rows by columns. For the worked example, a 3 m × 5 m rectangle gives 15 m² and a 2 m × 4 m rectangle gives 8 m², summing to 23 m². The sub-areas are ADDED (not multiplied) because area is additive.

activities.title: Cut the L-shaped floor plan into rectangles
feedback: If a cut leaves the corner region inside both pieces, that overlap is double-counted — shade the two pieces in different colours and check that no tile is both colours.
If the child multiplies the two sub-areas (e.g. 15×8) instead of adding, point back to the grid: each rectangle covers a separate set of tiles, so the tile counts are summed, giving 15 + 8 = 23.
If the total differs after a second split, re-check for a gap or overlap: valid non-overlapping splits must give the same total.
If the answer is written as '23 m' rather than '23 m²', relabel: area is counted in square units, not length units.
activities.rationale: Decomposing is a spatial act with concrete consequences: an overlapping cut double-counts the shared corner, and a different valid cut lands on the same total. Drawing and re-cutting makes additivity something the child discovers, and prompting why the pieces are added (not multiplied) names the additive principle explicitly.
sourceClaims: For 3.MD.7d, real-world area problems involve figures that are not all rectangular but decomposable into rectangles (e.g. an 'L-shaped' room); students recognise area as additive and find such areas by decomposing and adding.
Area is additive: the area of the union of two regions that overlap only at their boundaries is the sum of their areas; area is measured by tiling without gaps or overlaps.
Pupils find the area of rectilinear/compound shapes by counting or by splitting into rectangles at Key Stage 2.
learnerActions: Look at an L-shaped room on a grid with its outer measurements labelled.
Draw a cut line to split the shape into two non-overlapping rectangles.
Find each sub-rectangle's area by multiplying its sides (e.g. 3×5 = 15 m² and 2×4 = 8 m²).
Add the two areas to get the total, keeping square-metre units (23 m²).
Say why the two areas are ADDED rather than multiplied: each rectangle covers a separate part of the floor, and area is additive.
Re-cut the same shape a different valid way and confirm the total is still 23 m².
activities.intendedInsight: A rectilinear figure can be split into non-overlapping rectangles whose areas ADD to the whole; the pieces are summed (not multiplied) because area is additive, and any valid split gives the same total.

activities.title: Find the hidden internal side
feedback: If the child stalls at the blank side, prompt: 'Which outer measurements tell you this hidden length?'
If a number is invented rather than computed, show the subtraction that produces it (e.g. 5 − 3 = 2 for that illustrative figure, or 5 − 2 = 3 / 7 − 3 = 4 for the 23 m² plan).
activities.rationale: Deriving missing internal lengths is a distinct hurdle from partitioning; isolating it as a strategy prompt (not a concept reteach) targets children who freeze at an unprinted side.
sourceClaims: For 3.MD.7d, real-world area problems involve figures that are not all rectangular but decomposable into rectangles (e.g. an 'L-shaped' room); students recognise area as additive and find such areas by decomposing and adding.
learnerActions: Look at a compound shape (which may be a separate illustrative figure, not the earlier floor plan) where one internal side is left blank and only the outer measurements are printed.

Work out which outer measurements determine the missing internal length by subtracting; for example, 5 − 3 = 2 is a generic illustration of taking one printed outer length from another, not the derivation of a hidden side in the 23 m² floor plan (whose hidden sides come from 5 − 2 = 3 and 7 − 3 = 4).
Mark the derived length on the figure.
Complete the decomposition and compute the total area.
activities.intendedInsight: A sub-rectangle's unlabelled side can be derived by reasoning about the outer lengths, not guessed or taken only from printed numbers.

activities.title: Spot the whole-rectangle error
feedback: If the child accepts 35 m², overlay a grid and count the corner tiles that are missing from the figure.
If the child multiplies every printed number, ask which rectangle each number belongs to; the shape is two separate rectangles, not one product.
Reinforce: cut the figure into rectangles, then multiply each piece, then add.
activities.rationale: The whole-rectangle error (treating a compound shape as one big rectangle, or multiplying all numbers) is the signature misconception; confronting it on a fresh case surfaces and corrects it. Grid counting grounds the point concretely.
sourceClaims: Spatial structuring (seeing a region as rows and columns of squares) is the key hurdle and must be built with many array activities; discussions must distinguish area from length — grounding the overlap and add-the-edges errors.
learnerActions: Examine a worked solution where someone multiplied the outer bounding dimensions (e.g. 5×7 = 35 m²) as if the notch weren't there, or multiplied every printed number together.
Explain what that person forgot about the shape.
Overlay or imagine a grid and count: the tiles in the missing corner are not there.
Give the correct total by decomposing first (15 + 8 = 23 m²).
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying the outer bounding dimensions — or multiplying all the printed numbers together — counts tiles the shape does not contain; the missing notch must be accounted for, and here we do that by decomposing the shape into rectangles before multiplying each piece.

activities.title: Covering versus going around
feedback: If the child sums the edges, tile a sub-rectangle and have them count the square units inside instead.
If the square unit is dropped, relabel the total with m².
activities.rationale: Some children add side lengths or drop the square unit, conflating area with perimeter. Contrasting covering with going around, and counting actual tiles, distinguishes the two quantities.
sourceClaims: Spatial structuring (seeing a region as rows and columns of squares) is the key hurdle and must be built with many array activities; discussions must distinguish area from length — grounding the overlap and add-the-edges errors.
learnerActions: Tile one sub-rectangle and count the square units inside it.
Contrast that with tracing around the edges of the whole figure.
State whether the task asks for area (tiles inside) or perimeter (distance around), and answer with the correct square units.
activities.intendedInsight: Area counts the squares covering the inside and is reported in square units; adding up the edges gives a perimeter-like total, which is a different quantity.

constraints: Insist the two pieces are non-overlapping — shade them different colours and check no tile belongs to both; non-overlapping is exactly what lets the areas add.
Keep square units on every sub-area and on the total.

A static tap-to-reveal figure (reveal the dashed split, then each sub-area, then a lift-the-flap total) can explain the method, but does not let the child attempt their own cut or catch an overlap they created; use it as an explanatory scaffold, not as the main construction task.
Keep the figures flat rectilinear plans. Adding a third dimension drifts toward volume and obscures the decomposition, so a 3D treatment is not suited to this specific objective.

A scripted in-role dialogue does not itself elicit the child drawing a cut, computing each sub-area and summing; if used, let it frame or discuss the task rather than replace the hands-on construction. This is a scope note, not a claim that dialogue is inherently unable to teach the procedure.

Recognition-only formats (matching a shape to a valid decomposition, picking the 35 m² distractor) can assess and reinforce, but do not by themselves elicit the child independently drawing a cut and deriving a missing length.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic checked: 3×5 = 15, 2×4 = 8, 15+8 = 23 m²; the whole-rectangle distractor 5×7 = 35 m² is intentionally the wrong answer and must never be presented as correct. The 23 m² figure is self-consistent with a 5 m × 7 m bounding box (35 m²) and a 3 m × 4 m notch (12 m²), since 35 − 12 = 23.

The derived length '5 − 3 = 2' is a generic illustration only. In the specific 23 m² figure the hidden internal sides derive as 5 − 2 = 3 or 7 − 3 = 4, so if 'Find the hidden internal side' is deployed on the same shape its numbers must be relabelled for consistency.

Teachers should ensure the printed outer measurements of any specific figure are self-consistent with the intended decomposition, the one blank internal side, and the bounding box used for the distractor before use.
The objective covers both L- and T-shapes; the activities use an L-shape as the representative worked figure, and a T-shaped plan is an equally valid example to vary with.
One cited claim (National Curriculum KS2) was marked unverified in the source; it is retained as supporting the general splitting-into-rectangles approach, not as independent evidence of efficacy.

'How did you work out this side when it wasn't written on the plan?'
'Someone got 35 m² by doing 5×7. What did they forget about the shape?' (surfaces the whole-rectangle error on a fresh case)
'Why do we ADD the two areas together, and not multiply them?'

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: Area of Triangles & Parallelograms
topic.description: Find the area of parallelograms and triangles by relating them to rectangles: rearrange a parallelogram (cut off a triangle and move it) into a rectangle with the same base and perpendicular height; see a right triangle as half of a rectangle and any triangle as half of a parallelogram (or as two right triangles); use the resulting formulae A = b × h for parallelograms and A = ½ × b × h for triangles, always using the perpendicular height rather than a slanted side, including when the height falls outside an obtuse triangle; and recognise when an area formula can be used (rectangles, parallelograms, triangles) and when another method is needed, such as counting or estimating squares for an irregular shape
evidence: Cut a right-angled triangle off one end of a parallelogram with base 8 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm, move it to the other end to make an 8 cm × 5 cm rectangle, and state the area as 40 cm²

Show that a right triangle with legs 6 cm and 4 cm is half of a 6 cm × 4 cm rectangle (12 cm²), and that an obtuse triangle with base 12 cm and perpendicular height 7 cm, drawn outside the triangle, is half of a parallelogram (42 cm²)

Decide that a formula gives the area of a parallelogram with base 10 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm (50 cm², not the 60 cm² from its slanted 6 cm side) but not of an irregular leaf shape, whose area must be estimated by counting squares
topic.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is cutting triangular pieces of cloth where the base is 8 cm and the height is 5 cm, can they use a formula to work out the area of each piece?

pedagogy.summary: Children extend rectangle area to parallelograms (A = base × perpendicular height) and triangles (A = ½ × base × perpendicular height). The formulae are best DERIVED, not told: a parallelogram is cut and rearranged into a rectangle of equal area, and two identical triangles join to make a parallelogram or rectangle, so a triangle is half of it — which is why we divide by two. The load-bearing ideas are that the height must be the PERPENDICULAR distance to the base (not a slant side), that any side can serve as the base with its matching perpendicular height, and that the halving step follows from the dissection rather than being an arbitrary rule.
bestPractices: Derive each formula by dissection: rearrange a parallelogram into a rectangle; join two copies of a triangle into a parallelogram so the triangle is half of it.
Insist the height is perpendicular to the chosen base; have children mark the right angle and show non-examples of lines that are NOT the perpendicular height.
Include shapes in varied orientations so children see the base need not be horizontal and any side can be the base with its own perpendicular height.
Deliberately give diagrams with a decoy slant length (e.g. base 7, height 6, slant 8) so children practise selecting the perpendicular height and ignoring unnecessary numbers.
Tie the ÷2 to the two-triangles-make-a-parallelogram image so halving is meaningful and not forgotten.
keyRepresentations: Parallelogram cut-and-rearranged into a rectangle
Two congruent triangles joined into a parallelogram/rectangle
Right-angle mark showing base–height perpendicularity
Rotated shapes with base and perpendicular height labelled
Decoy-slant diagrams (extra unnecessary length shown)
commonMisconceptions: Uses the slant side instead of the perpendicular height, partly from believing every number given must be used.
Forgets to halve for a triangle (computes base × height and stops).
Thinks the base must be the horizontal or bottom side, so cannot identify base and height in rotated or obtuse triangles.

learn.summary: Year 6 learners derive and apply area formulae for parallelograms (A = base × perpendicular height) and triangles (A = ½ × base × perpendicular height) through dissection rather than being told the rules. A parallelogram is cut and rearranged into an equal-area rectangle; two congruent triangles are joined into a parallelogram so a triangle is seen to be exactly half (justifying the ÷2). The load-bearing ideas are: the height must be the PERPENDICULAR distance to the chosen base (not a slant side), any side can be the base with its own matching perpendicular height, and the halving step follows from the dissection rather than being an arbitrary rule. Decoy slant lengths teach that a 'given' number is not always a 'needed' number.

activities.title: Dissection workbench: rearrange to reveal the formulae
feedback: If the rearranged pieces form a rectangle of equal area, confirm that base × perpendicular height must therefore be the parallelogram's area.
When two congruent triangles snap into a parallelogram, point out that one triangle is exactly half, so we halve the product — this is why the ÷2 is there, not an arbitrary rule.
If a learner uses the slant side, mark the right angle and show the height must meet the base at 90°; the slant is longer and does not measure the perpendicular distance.

If a learner is stuck because the base is not at the bottom, rotate the shape and show any side can serve as the base with its own perpendicular height: for a triangle, this runs to the opposite vertex (or meets the extended base line if the triangle is obtuse); for a parallelogram, it runs to the opposite side.
activities.rationale: The national curriculum expects pupils to relate rectangle area to parallelograms and triangles by dissection and to understand the formulae, and the NCETM spine derives the ÷2 from joining two congruent triangles. A hands-on or on-screen rearrangement makes the derivation and the perpendicular-height requirement visible rather than told.
sourceClaims: Year 6 statutory: 'calculate the area of parallelograms and triangles'. Non-statutory: pupils 'relate the area of rectangles to parallelograms and triangles, for example, by dissection, and calculate their areas, understanding and using the formulae (in words or symbols) to do this'.

Area of parallelogram = base × perpendicular height; triangle = base × perpendicular height ÷ 2. Teachers must 'include examples of lines that are not the perpendicular height' and 'remind children that the line must be at 90° to the base'; show the base 'is not necessarily from the horizontal plane, and that any of the sides can be used as the base'; a 'who is right?' task uses a triangle with sides 8, 6 (perpendicular height) and 10 (slant); the ÷2 is derived because 'two triangles that are the same can be joined to make a parallelogram'; 'children may forget to halve after multiplying the base and the perpendicular height'.
learnerActions: Take a parallelogram whose perpendicular height from a top corner lands on the base. Cut along that height to remove a right-angled triangle, then slide it to the other end so it forms a rectangle of the SAME area. Confirm that base × perpendicular height is the area, because the rectangle's length and width are the parallelogram's base and perpendicular height.
Take a triangle, duplicate and rotate the copy, and fit the two copies together into a parallelogram; observe that the single triangle is exactly HALF, so its area is base × perpendicular height ÷ 2.
Place or drag the height line so it meets the base at 90°, marking the right angle; check a line that is NOT perpendicular and explain why it is not the height.
Rotate the shape so the base is no longer horizontal, then identify which side is now the base and where its perpendicular height falls.
Work with a diagram that includes a decoy slant length (e.g. base 7, perpendicular height 6, slant 8) and deliberately ignore the slant when computing the area.
activities.intendedInsight: The area formulae are consequences of rearranging shapes: a parallelogram is a rectangle in disguise, and a triangle is half a parallelogram, which is where the ÷2 comes from. The height is always perpendicular to whichever side is chosen as the base, and not every given number is needed.

activities.title: Paper-and-scissors dissection (hands-on alternative)
feedback: Because the rectangle is made from exactly the same pieces with no gaps or overlaps, it has the same area as the parallelogram; if the measured rectangle length and width match the parallelogram's base and perpendicular height (allowing for small measuring and cutting errors), that shows why base × perpendicular height gives the area.
If a learner draws the height to a slanted side rather than perpendicular to the base, have them use a right-angle check and redraw to the opposite vertex.
activities.rationale: Paper dissection achieves the same curriculum-specified derivation as an on-screen workbench and offers a tactile route; both make the rearrangement something the learner performs rather than watches. Paper cutouts have slight real thickness, so treat them as approximations of the ideal flat (zero-thickness) figures they represent.
sourceClaims: Year 6 statutory: 'calculate the area of parallelograms and triangles'. Non-statutory: pupils 'relate the area of rectangles to parallelograms and triangles, for example, by dissection, and calculate their areas, understanding and using the formulae (in words or symbols) to do this'.
learnerActions: Cut out a paper parallelogram, draw its perpendicular height, snip along it to remove a right-angled triangle and slide it across to physically make a rectangle; measure the rectangle's length and width and compare them with the parallelogram's base and perpendicular height.
Cut two identical paper triangles and fit them together to make a parallelogram or rectangle; state in words why one triangle is half.
Physically turn a triangle so a different side is the base, then draw the perpendicular height from the opposite vertex to that base and mark the right angle.
activities.intendedInsight: Physically cutting and rearranging makes the equal-area and 'half of a parallelogram' relationships concrete, and turning the paper shape shows the base does not have to be horizontal.

activities.title: 'Who is right?' and calculation practice with decoy lengths
feedback: If a learner reaches for the 8 cm slant, point to the right-angle mark: only the length perpendicular to the base measures the height; the slant is extra information.
If a learner stops at 7 × 6 = 42 for a triangle, send them back to the two-triangles image: one triangle is half, so halve to get 21 cm².
If a learner halves a parallelogram, show that a parallelogram IS the whole rectangle-equivalent, so no halving — the ÷2 belongs only to the triangle.
activities.rationale: Calculation items with decoy slants and 'who is right?' prompts directly surface the slant-height and forgot-to-halve errors flagged in the curriculum guidance. This activity checks and consolidates fluency; it is weaker at building the dissection insight, so it should follow the derivation work.

learnerActions: Compute the area of a triangle given a base, a marked perpendicular height and a decoy slant length, choosing the correct length and halving (e.g. base 7, perpendicular height 6, slant 8 → 7 × 6 ÷ 2 = 21 cm²).
Compute the area of a triangle with base 12 cm and perpendicular height 7 cm, halving the product: 12 × 7 ÷ 2 = 42 cm².
Decide in a 'who is right?' task which of two learners picked the correct length for the height, and justify the choice using the right-angle mark.

Complete a worked step that forces the ÷2 explicitly, and separately compute a parallelogram area without halving (e.g. base 8, perpendicular height 5 → 40 cm²) to show that ÷2 is NOT applied to parallelograms.

activities.title: Diagnostic: two shapes with decoy slants
feedback: Correct responses: triangle = 7 × 6 ÷ 2 = 21 cm²; parallelogram = 8 × 5 = 40 cm². Probe with 'why divide by two for the triangle but not the parallelogram?' and 'why didn't you use the 8 cm?'
